title: API 510 Training in Tulsa, OK: Vessel Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 510 exam prep for Tulsa vessel inspectors: refinery drums and columns, exchanger shops and Oklahoma's owner-user rule, with instructor Q&A.
h1: API 510 Training in Tulsa: Pressure Vessel Inspector Exam Prep for Refinery, Fabrication-Shop and Contract Inspectors
html:
API 510 exam prep in a city that builds pressure equipment as well as inspecting it

Most cities that employ API 510 inspectors do so because they have refineries and chemical plants. Tulsa has a refinery, and it also has a manufacturing base that turns out the equipment process plants run on. Chart Industries says it engineers and manufactures air-cooled heat exchangers in Tulsa, as well as in Beasley, Texas, under its Hudson Products, Air-X-Changers and Smithco brands. A Tulsa candidate for the pressure vessel inspector examination may therefore come from a refinery inspection department, from a contract inspection company that covers plants across Oklahoma, or from a shop floor where vessels and exchangers are built to ASME Section VIII.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Tulsa. The API 510 course is studied online at your own pace, and an instructor answers your questions along the way, so preparation fits around shift rotations and turnaround work. The American Petroleum Institute decides who is eligible, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification to those who pass. Atlantis holds no API approval as a training provider, and a finished course is preparation for the exam, not a credential.

Inside HF Sinclair's two Tulsa plants

HF Sinclair's Tulsa refinery is really two plants about two miles apart. Holly Corporation bought the west facility from Sunoco in June 2009 and the east facility from Sinclair later that year, and its annual report for 2009 described interconnect pipelines that would let intermediate streams move between them. HF Sinclair now gives the combined refinery a crude capacity of 125,000 barrels per day, running mainly sweet crude with up to 10,000 barrels per day of sour Canadian crude. EIA's refinery capacity survey, which reports each plant as of the start of 2026, still lists them separately: Tulsa East at 70,300 and Tulsa West at 85,000 barrels per calendar day of crude distillation capacity.

The equipment differs from one plant to the other, and so does the vessel work. EIA credits Tulsa East with a fluid catalytic cracker of 28,000 barrels per stream day, a catalytic reformer, naphtha, gasoline and diesel hydrotreating, alkylate and isomer production, and sulfur recovery. Tulsa West has vacuum distillation, a delayed coker of 9,300 barrels per stream day and the specialty side of the business. HF Sinclair says the site makes base oils, specialty process oils, horticultural oils, asphalt modifiers and wax, and Holly's 2009 report listed propane deasphalting, lube extraction and MEK dewaxing among the west plant's units.

UnitVessels an API 510 inspector meets thereQuestions the service raises
Crude and vacuum distillationTowers, overhead accumulators, desalters, exchanger shellsOverhead corrosion, insulated shells, static head on tall towers
Fluid catalytic cracker (east plant)Reactor, regenerator, main fractionator, gas plant drumsErosion, and wet H2S damage in the gas plant
Hydrotreaters and reformerReactors, high-pressure separators, feed and effluent exchangersHigh-temperature hydrogen attack and H2/H2S corrosion
Delayed coker (west plant)Coke drums, coker fractionator, blowdown drumSevere thermal cycling, which falls outside the mechanisms the exam lists
Lube extraction, dewaxing and deasphalting (west plant)Solvent recovery drums, chillers, filtrate and propane vesselsLow-temperature service, minimum design metal temperature and brittle fracture
Sulfur recovery, amine and sour water (east plant)Amine contactors and regenerators, sour water drumsAmine stress corrosion cracking and wet H2S damage

Read the table as a guide to what the job will ask of you, not as a list of what the examination contains. The examination draws its damage mechanism questions only from the RP 571 sections named in the Body of Knowledge, and the course follows that list.

Ponca City, Wynnewood and Ardmore: the rest of Oklahoma's refining

Tulsa-based contract inspectors seldom work only in Tulsa. EIA's 2026 survey counts five operating refineries in Oklahoma with 543,800 barrels per calendar day of crude capacity between them. Phillips 66's Ponca City refinery is the largest, at 228,000 barrels per calendar day, with a cat cracker of 69,935 barrels per stream day, a delayed coker of 27,730 and lubricant production capacity of its own. Valero's Ardmore refinery, at 86,000 barrels per calendar day, is the one Oklahoma plant with hydrocracking capacity in the survey, and CVR's Wynnewood refinery, at 74,500, runs a cat cracker and produces aromatics. Each brings its own vessels: hydrocracking means high-pressure reactors and separators in hydrogen service, and coking brings drums and fractionators with a long thermal history.

Oklahoma's boiler and pressure vessel law, and the owner-user inspector

Pressure equipment in Oklahoma falls under the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act, which the Department of Labor administers. The department says its jurisdiction covers boilers and other pressure vessels, that all inspectors must be commissioned by the National Board of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Inspectors, and that a certificate of operation follows once an inspection report shows compliance. Two parts of the Act matter to an API 510 candidate.

  • The three-year internal rule has an API exception. Section 141.13 of Title 40 calls for an internal inspection every three years, where construction permits, on pressure vessels subject to internal corrosion, but it excludes vessels within the scope of the API Pressure Vessel Inspection Code from that requirement.
  • Owner-user inspection is written into the law. The same section lets an owner or user inspect its own vessels if its inspection service is regularly established, supervised by people the Labor Commissioner finds qualified, and carried out under the National Board Inspection Code or the API code, as applicable. Section 141.14 then requires such a company to keep a file listing each vessel with its last and approximate next inspection dates, and to file a signed yearly statement giving the number of vessels it inspected.

That is the practical reason API 510 matters to Oklahoma plant inspectors: an owner-user organisation that takes the API route works to API 510, and the people in it are expected to know the code in detail. An API certificate is not a National Board commission, though. An inspector who also inspects for the jurisdiction or for an insurer needs the commission the state requires. Atlantis's guide to the owner-user inspection organisation explains how such a department is usually set up.

Damage mechanisms on the Tulsa job and on the exam

The current API 510 Body of Knowledge limits RP 571 questions to the definitions and fifteen mechanisms: amine stress corrosion cracking, atmospheric corrosion, boiler water and steam condensate corrosion, brittle fracture, caustic corrosion, caustic stress corrosion cracking, chloride stress corrosion cracking, corrosion under insulation, erosion, high-temperature H2/H2S corrosion, high-temperature hydrogen attack, hydrochloric acid corrosion, naphthenic acid corrosion, sulfidation and wet H2S damage. Several of them map straight onto Tulsa equipment.

  • Cold solvent service. Dewaxing chills oil and solvent well below ambient temperature, so vessels in that duty raise questions about minimum design metal temperature and impact testing, which is where brittle fracture and Figure UCS-66 meet.
  • Hydrogen at temperature. Hydrotreater reactors and their effluent exchangers are the places where high-temperature hydrogen attack and H2/H2S corrosion are assessed.
  • Sour streams. The sour Canadian share of the crude slate, the cat cracker's gas plant and the sulfur recovery train together bring wet H2S damage and amine cracking into the vessel programme.
  • Insulated shells. Insulated towers and drums can trap water from rain, storms and condensation in any climate. RP 571 sets out the operating temperatures at which carbon and austenitic stainless steels are most at risk, so learn the ranges from the text.

Mechanisms the exam leaves out, such as the thermal fatigue a coke drum lives with, still decide how your own equipment is inspected, so read beyond the listed sections for your unit.

Worked example: which corrosion rate after a change of feed?

API 510 asks the inspector to compare the long-term and short-term corrosion rates and to choose the one that best reflects current conditions, and the examination likes questions in which the two disagree. Take a hypothetical drum whose feed changed six years ago, when the unit began running a different blend.

  • Thickness when the drum entered service 30 years ago: 0.750 in.
  • Reading at the inspection six years ago: 0.708 in.
  • Reading today: 0.672 in.
  • Required thickness of the shell at its MAWP, from UG-27: 0.610 in.

The long-term rate is (0.750 − 0.672) ÷ 30 = 0.0026 in. per year. The short-term rate is (0.708 − 0.672) ÷ 6 = 0.0060 in. per year, more than twice as fast. The remaining corrosion allowance is 0.672 − 0.610 = 0.062 in., so the remaining life is 23.8 years on the long-term rate but 10.3 years on the short-term rate.

Unless an RBI assessment justifies something else, Section 6 of API 510 limits the interval between internal or on-stream inspections to half the remaining life or 10 years, whichever is less. The long-term rate would allow 10 years; the short-term rate allows 5.2. Because the change of feed explains the faster loss, the short-term rate describes the drum as it now operates, and an inspector who chose the long-term figure would almost double the interval on the strength of conditions that no longer exist. In the exam, look for the phrase in the question that tells you the service has changed. Atlantis's note on long-term and short-term corrosion rates works through more cases.

Routes into API 510 from Tulsa jobs

API's eligibility rules combine education, the kind of work you did and who you did it for. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year of supervising or performing inspection. A two-year degree or certificate needs two years and a high school diploma three, in each case in the design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of pressure vessels with at least one of those years in inspection, while candidates without formal education need five years or more. The experience must fall within the last ten years and, in API's wording, be gained while employed by or under contract with an authorized inspection agency. The API 510 certification page sets out the detail.

  • Exchanger and vessel shop inspectors. Fabrication quality work teaches Section VIII construction thoroughly, and Section VIII is one of the codes the open-book half draws on. Whether shop years count toward eligibility is a separate matter, because a fabricator is not normally an authorized inspection agency, so ask API before you rely on them.
  • NDT technicians. UT thickness and shear-wave technicians on plant turnarounds already produce the data an API 510 inspector evaluates. Atlantis's NDT training for Tulsa is a separate ASNT-based course that can come first.
  • Operators and maintenance staff. Operating and repair experience counts on the two-year and high school routes, provided the year of inspection work is there as well.
  • Engineering graduates. A mechanical engineering degree, such as the BSME the University of Tulsa offers, puts you on the one-year route once you have a year of inspection behind you.

Studying for API 510 from Tulsa

Refinery turnarounds compress months of inspection into a few weeks, and a candidate who works them will lose study time while they run. Because the course has no class timetable, you can plan backwards from the exam window: heavy reading and calculation practice in the quieter months, short daily reviews of definitions and interval rules during an outage, then timed practice papers once it is over. You can send a question to the instructor whenever it comes up, which matters when you are working nights.

Practise the open-book half on PDFs rather than paper, because the test centre puts the code files on the computer and nothing you have marked up comes in with you. Learn the structure of Section VIII well enough to reach UG-27, UG-32, UW-12, UCS-66 and UG-99 without hunting, and know where API 510 keeps its definitions. Prometric lists test centres in and around Tulsa, so book a seat as soon as API confirms your eligibility rather than waiting for the window to open. The API 510 practice questions are a useful check before the timed papers.

Sponsoring vessel inspectors from a Tulsa plant, shop or contractor

Employers can enrol one inspector or several, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate studies around their own shifts and still applies to API individually with their own experience record, so an employer's main jobs are to confirm the experience each candidate claims and to arrange cover for the exam day. A contractor with inspectors at Tulsa, Ponca City and Ardmore can prepare all of them the same way without gathering them in one place.

faq.q: Is there an API 510 class I can attend in person in Tulsa?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Tulsa, and the API 510 course has no class timetable to attend: you study online at your own pace and send questions to an instructor as they arise. The examination itself is taken in person at a Prometric test centre after API accepts your application, and API issues the certificate to candidates who pass.

faq.q: Does Oklahoma require refinery pressure vessels to be inspected by an API 510 inspector?
faq.a: Oklahoma's Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act allows an owner or user to run its own inspection service under the National Board Inspection Code or the API Pressure Vessel Inspection Code, provided the Labor Commissioner finds the people supervising it qualified. An owner-user organisation that takes the API route works to API 510, which is why certified inspectors are what such departments look for. The statute itself does not say that every inspector must hold API 510 certification.

faq.q: I build air-cooled heat exchangers in a Tulsa shop. Will that help me with API 510?
faq.a: It will help with the construction side of the exam, because Section VIII design, welding and examination rules run through the open-book questions, and RP 572 covers how exchangers are inspected once they are in service. Whether your shop years count as qualifying experience is a separate question: API ties experience to an authorized inspection agency, so describe your role carefully on the application and ask API if you are unsure. If they do not count, plan to build qualifying years with an owner-user or contract inspection organisation.

faq.q: For static head questions, do I use the specific gravity of the crude or product in the vessel?
faq.a: No. The API 510 Body of Knowledge states that all static head is based on a specific gravity of 1.0 and gives the conversion factor of 0.433 psi per foot. Use it to add static head to the MAWP at a lower part of a vessel, or to work out the vessel's MAWP at the top from the ratings of its parts and their elevations. In the plant the real liquid matters, but in the exam a question about a crude tower still uses water.

faq.q: Are low-temperature dewaxing and propane vessels covered by the API 510 exam?
faq.a: The service is not named, but the questions it raises are examined. Brittle fracture is one of the RP 571 mechanisms in the Body of Knowledge, and the impact-test rules of Section VIII, including Figure UCS-66 and the exemptions in UG-20, belong to the calculation set. If you inspect cold-service vessels at a lube plant, those topics will feel familiar; practise reading the curves and their notes accurately, because small slips in governing thickness change the answer.

faq.q: Does an Oklahoma National Board commission replace API 510 certification?
faq.a: No, they are different credentials for different roles. A National Board commission lets an inspector carry out inspections for the jurisdiction or for an insurer, and the Oklahoma Department of Labor requires its inspectors to hold one. API 510 certification shows knowledge of the in-service inspection code that owner-user and contract inspectors apply. Some people hold both, depending on whether they inspect for the state, an insurer or a plant.

faq.q: Can a Tulsa contractor enrol a group of vessel inspectors?
faq.a: Yes. Groups are welcome, fees are quoted on request, and because the course is self-paced the contractor does not have to take inspectors off rotation for class days. Each inspector applies to API individually, chooses an exam window and books a test centre seat once API confirms eligibility, while the instructor answers each person's questions as their own study reaches them.
